title: Digestion and Absorption: Turning a Meal into Molecules Your Cells Can Use

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: The single chemistry of digestion is {{c1::hydrolysis}}: a water molecule splits a covalent bond, donating an -H to one new end and an -OH to the other.
cards.back: One water molecule is consumed per bond broken; water is a reactant, not just the solvent.
cards.quote: The single chemistry of digestion is hydrolysis: a water molecule splits a covalent bond and caps the two new ends
cards.section: One reaction, downhill but slow

cards.front: Which enzyme family hydrolyzes each food bond: the peptide bond, the glycosidic bond, and the ester bond?
cards.back: Peptide bonds: proteases. Glycosidic bonds: amylases and the brush-border disaccharidases. Ester bonds in fat: lipases.
cards.quote: One cut, three cutters: each enzyme family decides which bond it can reach.
cards.section: One reaction, downhill but slow

cards.front: Hydrolysis of food bonds is downhill (negative ΔG), and the gut is full of water. Why are digestive enzymes still needed?
cards.back: Downhill sets where the reaction ends, not how fast. Uncatalyzed, a peptide bond in neutral water lasts years to centuries; in about six hours in the gut, water alone would break fewer than one in a thousand.
cards.why: An enzyme makes a cut in milliseconds.
cards.quote: Slow: with no enzyme, a peptide bond in neutral water lasts years to centuries, and a glycosidic bond in starch lasts millions of years.
cards.section: One reaction, downhill but slow

cards.front: State the organizing rule of digestion: where is a food bond actually cut, and what does the body control?
cards.back: A bond is cut only where an active enzyme meets an exposed bond. The body controls both: it exposes bonds in the gut, and keeps switched off in the gland those enzymes whose targets sit beside them.
cards.quote: So a bond is cut only where an active enzyme meets an exposed bond, and digestion is the body controlling those two meetings.
cards.section: One reaction, downhill but slow

cards.front: What absorbable products does digestion leave from protein, from starch and sugars, and from fat?
cards.back: Protein: amino acids plus di- and tripeptides. Starch and sugars: monosaccharides. Fat: fatty acids with monoacylglycerols.
cards.quote: amino acids plus di- and tripeptides from protein, monosaccharides from starch and sugars, and fatty acids with monoacylglycerols from fat
cards.section: One reaction, downhill but slow

cards.front: Salivary and pancreatic alpha-amylase cleave only {{c1::alpha-1,4}} glycosidic bonds.
cards.back: Not beta links, and not the alpha-1,6 branch points.
cards.quote: Amylase reads two things about a glycosidic bond: which way it points (alpha, not beta) and where it joins (carbon 4, not carbon 6).
cards.section: Carbohydrate: the enzyme's shape picks the bond

cards.front: Cellulose and starch are both pure glucose polymers. Cellulose is incubated with alpha-amylase. What happens, and why can humans live on starch but not cellulose?
cards.back: Nothing is cut: every link in cellulose is beta-1,4, and amylase cuts only alpha-1,4 bonds. Starch is alpha-linked, so amylase can cut it; cellulose stays intact.
cards.quote: That is why we live on starch but not on cellulose, though both are pure glucose polymers.
cards.section: Carbohydrate: the enzyme's shape picks the bond

cards.front: Amylopectin is digested first with alpha-amylase alone, then a brush-border enzyme extract is added. Predict the products after each step.
cards.back: After amylase: oligosaccharides and limit dextrins, because the alpha-1,6 branch points survive. After the brush-border enzymes (alpha-glucosidase, alpha-dextrinase): free glucose.
cards.quote: Brush-border enzymes finish the job: alpha-glucosidase and alpha-dextrinase, plus sucrase and lactase splitting the disaccharides.
cards.section: Carbohydrate: the enzyme's shape picks the bond

cards.front: How does SGLT1 move glucose into the enterocyte against its concentration gradient?
cards.back: Secondary active transport: glucose (or galactose) moves uphill, paid for by sodium flowing downhill. The basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase keeps the sodium gradient up.
cards.quote: SGLT1 carries glucose and galactose in by secondary active transport: uphill for the sugar, paid for by sodium flowing downhill.
cards.section: Carbohydrate: the enzyme's shape picks the bond

cards.front: GLUT5 carries fructose into the enterocyte by {{c1::facilitated diffusion}}, so fructose can move only down its gradient.
cards.quote: GLUT5 carries fructose by facilitated diffusion, so it can move fructose only down its gradient.
cards.section: Carbohydrate: the enzyme's shape picks the bond

cards.front: GLUT2 in the basolateral membrane is a passive transporter. Why can it still carry glucose out of the enterocyte to the blood?
cards.back: SGLT1 has already piled glucose up inside the cell, so from the cell the blood is downhill.
cards.quote: It is passive too, and that works because SGLT1 has already piled glucose up inside the cell: from there, the blood is downhill.
cards.section: Carbohydrate: the enzyme's shape picks the bond

cards.front: Ouabain is applied to a segment of small intestine. Which apical sugar uptake stalls, which continues, and why?
cards.back: Glucose and galactose uptake by SGLT1 stalls; fructose uptake by GLUT5 largely continues. Ouabain poisons the Na+/K+-ATPase, the sodium gradient runs down, and SGLT1 depends on it while GLUT5 is passive and not sodium-coupled.
cards.quote: The sodium gradient is kept up by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase (poison that pump with ouabain and SGLT1 stalls).
cards.section: Carbohydrate: the enzyme's shape picks the bond

cards.front: A drug selectively blocks basolateral GLUT2 in enterocytes. Predict the effect on export of glucose, galactose and fructose to the blood.
cards.back: Export of all three sugars to the blood is impaired. GLUT2 is the exit door all three share.
cards.quote: GLUT2, in the basolateral membrane, is the door all three sugars leave through toward the blood.
cards.section: Carbohydrate: the enzyme's shape picks the bond

cards.front: The gastric H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump) drives stomach pH down to {{c1::1.5 to 2.5}}.
cards.quote: the gastric H+/K+-ATPase, the proton pump, drives the pH down to 1.5 to 2.5
cards.section: Protein: switch the enzyme on only in the gut

cards.front: Stomach acid does one job for each half of the digestion rule (exposed bond, active enzyme). What are the two jobs?
cards.back: It denatures dietary proteins, exposing their peptide bonds, and it switches pepsinogen on to pepsin.
cards.quote: It denatures dietary proteins, unfolding them so their peptide bonds are exposed.
cards.section: Protein: switch the enzyme on only in the gut

cards.front: How is pepsinogen in the stomach converted to active pepsin?
cards.back: Falling pH (fastest below about pH 3) releases the extra segment holding it off. The first pepsin molecules then cut more pepsinogen, so activation is autocatalytic. No separate enzyme is needed.
cards.quote: As the surrounding pH falls, and fastest below about pH 3, the extra segment that holds it off lets go.
cards.section: Protein: switch the enzyme on only in the gut

cards.front: When acidic, partly digested protein reaches the small intestine, what do secretin and CCK each trigger?
cards.back: Secretin: a flood of bicarbonate that neutralizes stomach acid. CCK: release of pancreatic enzymes and contraction of the gallbladder to squeeze out bile.
cards.quote: Secretin triggers a flood of bicarbonate that neutralizes the stomach acid.
cards.section: Protein: switch the enzyme on only in the gut

cards.front: Each pancreatic protease is made as a {{c1::zymogen}} (proenzyme), an inactive precursor with an extra stretch of polypeptide.
cards.quote: Each protease is made as a zymogen (or proenzyme), an inactive precursor with an extra stretch of polypeptide.
cards.section: Why the pancreas does not digest itself

cards.front: Why is trypsinogen inactive while its extra N-terminal stretch is attached?
cards.back: The active site is misshapen: the substrate pocket and the oxyanion hole that steadies the charged intermediate are not yet formed.
cards.quote: the pocket that holds the substrate and the spot that steadies the reaction's charged intermediate (the oxyanion hole) are not yet formed
cards.section: Why the pancreas does not digest itself

cards.front: Where is enteropeptidase located, what does it do, and why does its location protect the pancreas?
cards.back: It is anchored to the duodenal lining and makes one cut in trypsinogen, activating it. Because the switch sits on the gut wall, the first trypsin normally appears only in the intestine.
cards.quote: Because the switch sits on the gut wall, the first trypsin normally appears only where pancreatic juice meets the intestine.
cards.section: Why the pancreas does not digest itself

cards.front: Why is trypsin called the master switch of pancreatic enzyme activation?
cards.back: Trypsin cuts after lysine or arginine, and the activating bond of every pancreatic zymogen follows one, so trypsin activates them all, including more trypsinogen.
cards.why: One cut by enteropeptidase becomes a flood of active enzymes, all in the gut.
cards.quote: Trypsin cuts peptide bonds just after a lysine or an arginine, and the activating bond in every pancreatic zymogen follows one
cards.section: Why the pancreas does not digest itself

cards.front: Inside the pancreas, a few trypsinogen molecules switch on faster than the trypsin inhibitor can catch them. Predict what happens.
cards.back: Trypsin activates more trypsin and then the other zymogens, and the gland starts to digest itself. Premature activation is thought to be a key early step in acute pancreatitis.
cards.why: The trypsin loop amplifies anywhere, not only in the gut.
cards.quote: Premature trypsin activation inside the gland is thought to be a key early step in acute pancreatitis
cards.section: Why the pancreas does not digest itself

cards.front: A mutation abolishes the pancreatic trypsin inhibitor SPINK1. Predict the effect on the risk of pancreatic self-digestion, and name the rule.
cards.back: Risk should rise: stray trypsin made early is no longer caught, so the trypsin-makes-trypsin loop can start inside the gland.
cards.why: SPINK1 is the backup for zymogen storage; a loop that amplifies in the gut amplifies anywhere.
cards.quote: with a trypsin inhibitor made in the same cells (SPINK1) as backup to catch the odd molecule that switches on early
cards.section: Why the pancreas does not digest itself

cards.front: Duodenal fluid from an infant born without enteropeptidase has almost no protease activity. Enteropeptidase is added to the fluid in a tube. What happens, and what does it show?
cards.back: Trypsin activity appears. The pancreatic zymogens were secreted normally all along; only the activating switch was missing.
cards.quote: add enteropeptidase to it in a tube and trypsin activity appears: the zymogens were there all along, and only the switch was missing
cards.section: Why the pancreas does not digest itself

cards.front: Trypsin converts procolipase to colipase, a lipase helper. Why is triacylglycerol digestion still largely spared when trypsin never forms?
cards.back: Lipase is secreted already active, and uncut procolipase already does much of colipase's job, so trypsin's cut tunes fat digestion rather than enabling it.
cards.quote: Lipase itself is secreted already active, and uncut procolipase already does much of colipase's job, so trypsin's cut tunes fat digestion rather than enabling it.
cards.section: Colipase and why fat digestion survives without trypsin

cards.front: Why can the pancreas secrete amylase and lipase already active, while its proteases must be zymogens?
cards.back: Their targets are not in the granule: no starch (glycogen sits in the cytoplasm) and no triacylglycerol, and lipase works only at an oil-water surface. Proteases sit beside protein.
cards.quote: Their targets are not inside the granule, so they need no off switch.
cards.section: Why the pancreas does not digest itself

cards.front: Pepsinogen and trypsinogen are both zymogens. How do they differ in what holds them off and what switches them on?
cards.back: Trypsinogen's extra stretch holds the active site misshapen and enteropeptidase switches it on. Pepsinogen's extra stretch physically plugs the active site, and acid is the switch.
cards.quote: in pepsinogen it physically plugs the active site until acid releases it
cards.section: How a zymogen is held off

cards.front: Name the three sites where dietary protein is cut in the small intestine.
cards.back: The lumen (pancreatic proteases), the brush border (brush-border peptidases), and the cytoplasm of the enterocyte (intracellular peptidases).
cards.quote: The second and third sites are the brush border and the cell itself.
cards.section: Three sites of cutting

cards.front: The enterocyte transporter PepT1 is blocked. Which protein digestion products can still be absorbed, and which cannot?
cards.back: Intact di- and tripeptide uptake through PepT1 is lost; free amino acids made by brush-border peptidases can still use their own transporters.
cards.quote: the small peptides are absorbed intact through the transporter PepT1 and finished off by peptidases inside the cell
cards.section: Three sites of cutting

cards.front: A patient takes omeprazole, so stomach acid is suppressed. Predict the effect on gastric protein digestion, and say whether the pancreatic relay depends on acid.
cards.back: Gastric digestion falls: less acid means less denaturation and slower pepsinogen activation. The pancreatic zymogens are switched on by enteropeptidase, not acid, so that relay is not directly acid-dependent.
cards.why: Acid is a trigger for pepsinogen; the pancreatic relay and brush-border peptidases do not depend on it directly.
cards.quote: No separate enzyme is needed: acid is the trigger.
cards.section: Protein: switch the enzyme on only in the gut

cards.front: Bile salts split one 1 mm fat droplet into droplets 10 µm across, with the same total volume. By what factor does the total surface area rise?
cards.back: Number of droplets = (1000/10)^3 = 10^6; each has (10/1000)^2 = 10^-4 of the original area. Total area rises 10^6 x 10^-4 = 100-fold.
cards.why: At fixed volume, total area scales as original diameter divided by new diameter; 1 mm to 1 µm gives 1,000-fold.
cards.quote: multiplies the surface area 1,000-fold, and the surface is where lipase works
cards.section: Fat: the exposure problem

cards.front: Which ester bonds of a triacylglycerol does pancreatic lipase cleave, and what products does it leave?
cards.back: The two outer positions, sn-1 and sn-3, leaving a 2-monoacylglycerol and two free fatty acids.
cards.quote: It cleaves the ester bonds at the two outer positions (sn-1 and sn-3) to leave a 2-monoacylglycerol and two free fatty acids.
cards.section: Fat: the exposure problem

cards.front: Lipase products are packed into {{c1::micelles}}, tiny bile-salt bundles that ferry them through the watery layer to the enterocyte.
cards.quote: Those products are packed into micelles, tiny bile-salt bundles that ferry them through the watery layer to the cell.
cards.section: Fat: the exposure problem

cards.front: Why does the enterocyte spend energy rebuilding triacylglycerols from the fatty acids and monoacylglycerol it just absorbed?
cards.back: Rebuilding keeps their level inside low so more keep flowing in, stops free fatty acids acting as detergents, and makes cargo that can be packed into chylomicrons.
cards.quote: Rebuilding uses them up as they arrive, so their level inside stays low and more keep flowing in
cards.section: Fat: the exposure problem

cards.front: Why do chylomicrons leave the intestine through the lymph rather than blood capillaries?
cards.back: They are far larger than the openings in blood capillary walls but slip through the loose junctions of the lacteal, the lymph vessel at the center of each villus.
cards.quote: Chylomicrons are far larger than the openings in the wall of a blood capillary, but they can slip through the loose junctions
cards.section: Fat: the exposure problem

cards.front: Pancreatic enzyme delivery fails (as in cystic fibrosis) while stomach acid and bile are normal. Which nutrient fails worst, what sign shows it, and why?
cards.back: Fat; undigested fat appears in the stool (steatorrhea). Carbohydrate and protein have brush-border backups; fat has none, and pancreatic lipase is the principal triacylglycerol-digesting enzyme.
cards.quote: Fat has no brush-border backup: bile still emulsifies the droplets, and gastric lipase starts the job
cards.section: Fat: the exposure problem

cards.front: A meal contains a tracer-labeled medium-chain fatty acid. Where does the tracer first leave the intestine, and why not by the long-chain route?
cards.back: In the portal blood, toward the liver, carried on albumin. Medium-chain fatty acids are water-soluble enough not to need chylomicrons and the lymph.
cards.quote: short- and medium-chain fatty acids are water-soluble enough (medium-chain fatty acids ride on albumin) to leave for the portal blood and the liver
cards.section: Taking it up: where each piece goes

cards.front: In lactase deficiency, why does drinking milk cause diarrhea, gas and bloating?
cards.back: Undigested lactose stays in the gut and draws water after it (osmotic diarrhea, no immune attack). Gut bacteria ferment the lactose, producing gas and bloating.
cards.quote: Undigested lactose stays in the gut and draws water in after it, so the diarrhea is osmotic, with no immune attack involved.
cards.section: Clinical connections

cards.front: Omeprazole lasts only about an hour in the blood. Why does acid suppression last much longer?
cards.back: Activated by acid, it forms a covalent bond to the proton pump. Acid recovers only as the cell breaks that bond and makes new pumps.
cards.quote: The bond outlasts the drug in the blood, so acid stays suppressed until the cell makes new pumps.
cards.section: Clinical connections

cards.front: Gluten peptides resist complete digestion because they are rich in {{c1::proline}}, which kinks the backbone.
cards.back: They are also glutamine-rich. Celiac disease is autoimmune, not an allergy.
cards.quote: proline- and glutamine-rich gluten peptides that resist complete digestion (proline kinks the backbone)
cards.section: Clinical connections

cards.front: A patient with untreated celiac disease develops bloating and diarrhea after milk. Explain how the two conditions connect, and how the milk symptoms differ in cause from the celiac damage.
cards.back: Celiac damage flattens the villi, which can cause a secondary lactase deficiency. The milk symptoms are osmotic and from bacterial fermentation; the villus damage itself is immune.
cards.why: Lactase sits in the brush border; the lactose lane fails without any immune attack on lactose.
cards.quote: The damage flattens the villi, so absorption of many nutrients suffers, and celiac damage to the villi can cause a secondary lactase deficiency.
cards.section: What turns gluten resistance into celiac disease

cards.front: A gliflozin drug blocks SGLT2, the kidney's sodium-coupled glucose transporter. Predict the effect on urine glucose.
cards.back: Urine glucose rises: glucose the kidney would have taken back is dumped into the urine.
cards.quote: block it and glucose the kidney would have taken back is dumped into the urine
cards.section: SGLT2 and the gliflozins

cards.front: A digestive enzyme has a turnover of about 50 per second. How long does each cut take, and about how many bonds does one enzyme molecule cut in a minute?
cards.back: Time per cut = 1/50 s = 0.02 s = 20 ms. Cuts per minute = 50 x 60 = 3,000.
cards.quote: An enzyme with a turnover of about 50 per second makes a cut every 20 ms.
cards.section: How slow is slow?

cards.front: A gland stores a protease and a nuclease together in the same secretory granule, which holds protein but no RNA or DNA. Which enzyme must be made as a zymogen?
cards.back: Only the protease. Its target, protein, sits beside it in the granule; the nuclease has no target there, so it can be secreted active, like pancreatic ribonuclease.
cards.why: Any secreted enzyme whose target sits beside it in the granule must be built switched off.
cards.quote: The same logic covers pancreatic ribonuclease and deoxyribonuclease, also secreted active: the granule holds no RNA or DNA.
cards.section: Why the pancreas does not digest itself

cards.front: Compare enteropeptidase deficiency with pancreatic insufficiency (little pancreatic enzyme reaching the duodenum). Which nutrient fails worst in each, and why the difference?
cards.back: Enteropeptidase deficiency: protein, since no trypsin forms; fat and carbohydrate are largely spared. Pancreatic insufficiency: fat, since lipase itself is missing and fat has no brush-border backup.
cards.why: Only proteases need the trypsin switch; lipase is secreted active but has no substitute.
cards.quote: Triacylglycerol and carbohydrate digestion are largely spared: lipase is secreted active and uncut procolipase already helps it
cards.section: Why the pancreas does not digest itself
